reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents a purported tech-support scam as material for testing and explanation rather than making the offer to viewers. Although the tested caller requests a $150 transfer for computer repair, the recorded participant disputes the claim and the creator warns viewers not to trust such virus messages or buy unnecessary services. The video does not show the creator soliciting payment, credentials, or remote access from the audience.

Don't... don't listen to scammers trying to say you have a virus on your computer or anything like that.
You will transfer $150. Then I can fix up your computer
What I will do, I will connect your computer remotely with the server, so I can diagnose the problem behind.
you tried to sell me something that I didn't need because of a fake browser pop-up.

opening.argument: The video contains a complete payment-and-service solicitation, not merely an abstract warning. The caller claims to be a legitimate company, proposes remote access to diagnose the computer, asks which bank is available, and links a $150 transfer to fixing the alleged problem. That is a concrete action pathway: accept the claimed diagnosis, provide access or banking cooperation, and transfer money for the promised repair. The video therefore materially presents and demonstrates a scam acquisition flow, regardless of the creator's later commentary.

citations.quote: this time you're speaking with their legitimate company

Which bank do you have an account in?
You will transfer $150. Then I can fix up your computer

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense treats the caller's conduct as irrelevant because the creator does not personally request payment from viewers. But the video's central material is still a purported support representative linking remote access, bank information, and a $150 transfer to a promised repair. Calling this an investigation does not remove the solicitation or make the presented payment pathway legitimate. The warning comes only after the transaction pitch has been demonstrated.

citations.quote: you're gonna like remotely get into my computer

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted payment pathway belongs to the caller being tested, not to the video's audience. The creator does not ask viewers to transfer money, provide bank details, or grant remote access. Instead, the creator explicitly says the purpose is to show people how to identify scams and tells them not to listen to such claims. The existence of a scam inside an investigation does not turn the investigation into a solicitation.

citations.quote: I'm just trying to trying to show people on YouTube what these scams are about and how how to identify them?

opening.argument: The combination of impersonation, alarm, technical access, and payment is too specific to dismiss as ordinary support. The caller says the company is legitimate, claims the computer and network are damaged, offers remote diagnosis, asks about online banking, and demands $150 for a license and repair. The frames also show a Microsoft-branded support alert stating that the computer is blocked, displaying a phone number, and presenting a registration-key field. Together, these signals create a deceptive path from an alarming warning to money or sensitive access.

citations.quote: this time you're speaking with their legitimate company
There is an $150 charge.
We will give you the account number. You will transfer $150.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense acknowledges the $150 demand and remote-diagnosis pitch, but labels them merely third-party conduct without addressing the surrounding deception. The caller invokes Microsoft legitimacy, describes hidden network damage, seeks banking information, and ties payment to a fix. The Microsoft-branded blocked-computer screen and registration-key prompt reinforce the same pressure mechanism. A later warning does not undo the demonstrated deceptive sequence.

citations.quote: this time you're speaking with their legitimate company

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These signals establish that the caller is being exposed as deceptive, not that the creator is making the claim. The caller's request for $150 and remote access is directly challenged, and the creator explains that a browser pop-up is not a genuine system notification. The frames show the simulated alert as part of the demonstration; they do not show the creator endorsing it or asking the audience to submit a key or call the number.

If you're just going to a website and it pops up on your browser, like on your Internet Explorer or Chrome or anything, don't believe it

opening.argument: The educational framing can also function as promotion for the video's channel and its attention-generating scam encounter. The title foregrounds showing a scammer, the description says fake errors were shown to try to get $150, and the creator expressly directs viewers toward the YouTube presentation. The content packages a recognizable Microsoft-support identity, a blocked-computer scenario, and a money demand into an entertaining spectacle, while the description separately asks viewers to like, subscribe, and comment. That is not neutral documentation alone; it promotes participation around a scam-centered performance.

citations.quote: Showing a Tech Support Scammer My YouTube Channel
He decided it would be a good idea to show Samuel fake errors to try to get $150.
If you enjoyed be sure to hit that like button and subscribe for future content!
I would like to see your youtube channel

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense relies on the creator's stated warning but overlooks how the video packages the scam interaction as channel-centered entertainment. Its title highlights the creator's YouTube channel, the description links the fake errors to obtaining $150, and the creator asks viewers to like, subscribe, and comment. The warning may coexist with promotion: it does not prove that the presentation is purely neutral or detached from participation incentives.

citations.quote: Showing a Tech Support Scammer My YouTube Channel
If you enjoyed be sure to hit that like button and subscribe for future content!
I would like to see your youtube channel

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The title and engagement request promote the channel, not a paid support service, payment transfer, or access scheme. The description accurately characterizes fake errors used to test the caller, while the creator's closing statement tells viewers to end the task and reject browser-based virus claims. Nothing here asks viewers to buy, register, deposit, or contact the caller; the surrounding framing identifies the conduct as a scam.
